Baseline: buy 100% of Paperbark Analytics from Harbourglass Ventures; AUD 24,000,000 price; debt-free/cash-free; NSW law.

=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

## Overall assessment

**Do not accept this package as drafted.** The Seller combines broad disclosures and deemed Buyer knowledge with restrictions applying to virtually every claim. That could leave Wattlebridge bearing known risks while also losing meaningful recourse for undisclosed liabilities.

The agreed baseline remains **AUD 24 million for 100% of Paperbark, debt-free/cash-free, under NSW law**. The Seller’s statements that matters are “addressed”, “ordinary course” or “settled” do not establish that the underlying risks have been resolved.

This review is based on the supplied update and Disclosure Letter—not the underlying DD documents or complete SPA. The points below therefore distinguish established gaps from matters requiring verification.

## 1. Liability and recourse: reject the blanket general regime

### Cap, thresholds and time limits

The proposed **AUD 4.8 million general warranty cap** is only 20% of price. Whether that is commercially acceptable depends on diligence, recoverability and the remaining protections. **It is not acceptable as a cap for all transaction risks.**

Push for a clear, overriding allocation:

| Claim category | Buyer position |
|---|---|
| General business warranties | Negotiate a higher cap and longer notification period; 24–36 months is a sensible opening position. |
| Fundamental warranties: capacity, authority, ownership and title | Separate protection, ordinarily up to at least the purchase price, with materially longer survival. |
| Tax warranties and tax covenant/indemnity | Separate regime aligned with relevant statutory assessment periods, extensions and a notification buffer. |
| Identified-risk indemnities | Express, risk-specific caps and survival periods; not automatically subject to general warranty restrictions. |
| Purchase-price adjustments, debt discharge, leakage and contractual payment obligations | Enforceable in full, outside the general warranty cap, basket and time bar. |
| Fraud and deliberate misconduct | Express carve-outs from contractual limitations, appropriately drafted. Preserve rights that cannot lawfully be excluded. |

**Why:** “All Claims unless expressly stated otherwise” could limit recovery of unpaid contractual amounts or undermine a supposedly specific indemnity. The carve-outs must work consistently across clauses 9.3, 12, 13 and 20.5, including the definition of “Claim”.

The proposed thresholds also favour the Seller:

- **AUD 25,000 de minimis:** lower it and aggregate related claims or claims arising from the same underlying cause.
- **AUD 250,000 deductible basket:** seek a tipping basket, so qualifying losses become recoverable from the first dollar once the threshold is crossed.
- Exclude fundamental, tax, identified-risk and payment claims from these thresholds.

Check whether timely notification preserves a claim until resolution, what detail a notice must contain, and whether a separate proceedings deadline could prematurely extinguish it.

### Exclusive remedy and non-reliance

Reject provisions applying indiscriminately to “all Claims of any nature”. They should not neutralise express indemnities, payment obligations, equitable relief or appropriate termination rights.

Preserve fraud claims and non-excludable statutory rights, including applicable Australian Consumer Law rights. Non-reliance wording can materially affect a misrepresentation case even where statutory liability cannot simply be excluded; it should not be treated as harmless boilerplate.

## 2. Disclosure and Buyer knowledge: prevent wholesale risk transfer

**The general disclosure of the entire data room and public records is too broad.** A fact being discoverable somewhere is not the same as a risk having been fairly explained.

Require:

- Disclosure sufficiently detailed to identify the **nature and scope** of the matter and its connection to the relevant warranty.
- A fixed, indexed, preserved disclosure bundle, with no automatic incorporation of later uploads.
- Narrowly defined public-record disclosures, rather than everything theoretically searchable.
- No automatic release from liability through supplemental disclosures. Material updates should trigger agreed Buyer remedies.

Reject clause 8.3’s constructive-knowledge test and attribution of all advisers’ knowledge. Seek **no knowledge exclusion**, or, as a fallback, only actual knowledge of specified Buyer individuals, without imputed knowledge or a duty of inquiry.

**Crucially, disclosed risks must remain covered by expressly negotiated indemnities, completion conditions and price protections.** Otherwise the disclosure could defeat the very protection obtained for that risk.

The 22 September snapshot also requires updating: obtain current evidence, not merely repetition of the historical disclosures.

## 3. Bluefen: consent is not yet established

Bluefen represents approximately **AUD 3.6 million, or 30% of FY26 revenue**, making this a critical completion risk.

The Disclosure Letter expressly says there is no final written consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied. “Reasonable endeavours” is not a substitute for the required outcome.

**Push for a Buyer-waivable condition precedent** requiring:

- Valid written consent addressing the transaction.
- Satisfaction of the associated contractual conditions.
- No unacceptable repricing, termination rights or other adverse changes.
- Supporting evidence satisfactory to the Buyer acting reasonably.

Include a long-stop date and termination right if the condition remains unmet. Delivery of a consent document alone should not deem the condition satisfied.

## 4. Riverlark: no unsecured promise of post-completion release

Approximately **AUD 3.2 million remains outstanding**, and no final security discharge is included.

A release “following Completion” could leave the acquired company indebted or its assets encumbered after the Buyer has paid.

Require a completion-linked payoff and discharge process:

- Current payout statement covering principal, interest, fees and break costs.
- Payment directly to the lender through the funds flow.
- Binding lender release arrangements effective at Completion, including relevant guarantees and security.
- Searches and subsequent registration evidence confirming the releases.

Reflect the debt in the agreed debt-free/cash-free mechanics **without double counting**. If registration steps necessarily follow Completion, the substantive discharge should already be secured through enforceable lender arrangements, not depend on Seller goodwill.

## 5. Completion bonuses: allocate the full economic cost

The **AUD 420,000 bonuses are conditional liabilities**, not necessarily presently payable debts. But completion may trigger them, making their omission from the funds flow material.

Require:

- Confirmation of each entitlement, continued-employment condition and payment date.
- Assessment of superannuation, payroll tax and other applicable on-costs.
- Express Seller economic responsibility through the agreed transaction-expense/debt-like adjustment or another clear mechanism.
- Correct payroll payment and withholding arrangements, plus protection against omitted amounts.

Calling them “a matter for the Seller” does not prevent Paperbark from owing employees after Completion. Avoid counting the same liability twice through working capital and transaction-expense adjustments.

## 6. Ironquay IP: paying SOW3 may not cure every title issue

The disclosed position is **not proof of non-payment**, but it exposes an unresolved chain-of-title risk: transfer apparently depends on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee, while AUD 180,000 is recorded as open and no receipt or confirmatory assignment is available.

Require verified payment status and, preferably before Completion:

- Evidence that all transfer conditions have been met.
- An effective confirmatory assignment covering the required materials and rights.
- Verification of relevant subcontractor rights and any necessary licences or moral-rights consents.

Reject an indemnity confined to the SOW3 payment itself. It should address losses arising from the identified ownership defect, including third-party claims, remediation and reasonable enforcement costs, with suitable survival and security. A payment-only indemnity does not ensure the Buyer acquires usable IP.

## 7. Export/privacy incident: investigate, do not assume either outcome

The material establishes an unintended external delivery, **not a confirmed notifiable data breach or quantified loss**. Equally, absence of confirmed access does not establish that no breach occurred.

Require prompt investigation of access logs, link security, recipients, affected data, containment and applicable legal/customer obligations. Assess notification requirements under applicable privacy law, including the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme where relevant.

Push for:

- Pre-completion containment and compliance covenants.
- Buyer visibility and consultation, without delaying legally required notifications.
- A specific indemnity for appropriate losses attributable to the pre-completion incident, with regulatory penalties covered only to the extent legally permissible.
- A materiality-based completion protection if investigation reveals serious consequences.

Do not accept the Seller’s unsupported “not expected to be material” conclusion.

## 8. Supplier renewals: assess the related AUD 330,000 together

The three AUD 110,000 renewals should be considered **in aggregate**, particularly for interim-conduct approval thresholds.

Obtain dates, scope, commercial necessity, termination rights and whether amounts are accrued, prepaid or newly committed. Ordinary operating costs are not automatically Seller liabilities or debt-like items. However, non-ordinary, accelerated or unapproved commitments may justify a price adjustment, indemnity or covenant remedy.

Prevent splitting related commitments to avoid Buyer-consent thresholds.

## 9. Lease and Mossvale: distinguish notice from consent

Do not impose unsupported requirements:

- **Office lease:** the supplied disclosure identifies notification, not landlord consent. Verify and satisfy the actual notice obligation.
- **Mossvale:** an assignment restriction does not, by itself, require consent to a share sale. Review the full agreement for separate change-control or deemed-assignment provisions.

Seek evidence of actual compliance rather than assuming either consent is required.

## 10. Share title and tax/IP warranties remain open

The share register is important evidence, **not a complete title investigation**. Verify issued capital, ownership history, certificates and transfers, options or convertibles, encumbrances, shareholder restrictions and required approvals. Require effective transfers of all shares free of encumbrances at Completion.

Separately, reject the statement that tax and IP warranties are “settled”. Tax needs dedicated pre-completion liability protection. IP warranties should address ownership, licences, infringement and relevant developer arrangements, subject to carefully negotiated disclosures—not merely the general short-form regime.

## Recommended negotiating priorities

1. **Make Bluefen consent and Riverlark discharge genuine completion protections.**
2. **Correct the funds flow** for debt, bonuses and applicable costs, with consistent definitions and no double counting.
3. **Resolve Ironquay title** and obtain meaningful incident protection.
4. **Replace blanket claim limitations** with separate fundamental, tax, indemnity and payment regimes.
5. **Reject data-room dumping and constructive Buyer knowledge.**
6. Obtain current supporting evidence and consider a **targeted retention, escrow or other security** for unresolved exposures and Seller recovery risk.

The central principle is simple: **disclosure identifies a risk; it does not resolve it or determine who should pay for it.**
